WASHINGTON (CNN) — If you pay close attention in the nation’s capital, you may detect sounds of outrage from a government watchdog organization monitoring congressional pork-barrel spending.

One item highlighted in the newly released “Pig Book” involves research into the smell of pigs. Citizens Against Government Waste issued its yearly “Pig Book” on Tuesday, identifying lawmakers the group views as the worst offenders when it comes to pork spending — House and Senate members who use earmarks to direct federal dollars toward projects in their own districts or states.

Appropriately, the report includes almost $1.8 million for research in Iowa on swine odor and manure management.

According to the organization’s Tuesday report, “In fiscal year 2009, Congress stuffed 10,160 projects into the 12 appropriations bills worth $19.6 billion.” That total represents a 14 percent rise from 2008.

The “Pig Book” also points to dozens of projects the group describes as especially clear examples of pork-barrel spending.

Tom Schatz, president of Citizens Against Government Waste, said taxpayers are nearing a breaking point. “Taxpayers are ready to revolt,” he said. “Despite repeated claims by members of Congress that earmarks have been reduced, the Pig Book belies that claim.”

Among the spending singled out was $3.8 million for the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy, an organization working to find a new purpose for the former home of the Detroit Tigers, where the team played from 1896 until 1999.

Another $1.9 million was directed to the Pleasure Beach water taxi service project in Bridgeport, Connecticut. That earmark was requested by then-Rep. Chris Shays. Because a bridge burned more than 10 years earlier, people going to the beach must travel a few additional miles to reach it.

Alaska ranked first in the country for pork spending per resident, at $322 per person. Arizona ranked last, with under $12 per person. Sen. John McCain does not seek earmarks for Arizona.

Mississippi Sen. Thad Cochran, the top Republican on the Senate Appropriations Committee, received the largest total amount of earmarks among senators, with $653 million. Sen. Daniel Inouye, Democrat of Hawaii and chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, ranked second with $445 million.

In the House, Democratic Reps. Neil Abercrombie and Mazie Hirono of Hawaii led the earmark list. Abercrombie’s favored projects received nearly $257 million, while Hirono’s received nearly $153 million.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, Democrat of Nevada, was given the group’s “Porkasaurus” award for securing $143,000 for the Las Vegas Natural History Museum.

“Sen. Reid is fond of saying that earmarks have been around since we were a country. Now he must be blaming it on the dinosaurs,” Schatz said.

Not everyone whose project received earmark funding accepted the label of “pork.” Kathleen Wendler, a board member of the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy, said the $3.8 million for the former stadium was essential to improving the surrounding Detroit neighborhood.

The funding “is not pork at all,” Wendler said. She argued that, if put to proper use, the ballpark could become an “economic development generator for the local business district.” She added that the project would help attract younger residents to the area and, over time, help preserve the neighborhood.

For a project to be included in the “Pig Book,” it must satisfy at least one of several criteria: it was sought by only one chamber of Congress; it lacked specific authorization; it was not awarded through competition; it was not requested by the president; it substantially surpassed either the president’s budget request or the prior year’s funding level; it did not receive congressional hearings; or it benefited only a local or special interest.

CNN’s Alan Silverleib contributed to this report.

## Watchdog group releases 2009 “Pig Book,” targeting congressional earmarks

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — A government watchdog group took aim at Congress on Tuesday, releasing its annual catalog of what it calls wasteful federal spending — a list that includes money for swine odor research, stadium redevelopment, a water taxi project and thousands of other earmarks tucked into spending bills.

Citizens Against Government Waste, a Washington-based advocacy group that has long criticized congressional earmarking, said its 2009 **“Congressional Pig Book”** identified **10,160 earmarks worth $19.6 billion** in the fiscal year’s appropriations bills.

The group said the projects show that, despite promises from lawmakers to curb earmarks and make the process more transparent, Congress continues to steer federal money to parochial projects with limited national benefit.

“Members of Congress are still bringing home the bacon,” the group said in releasing the report, arguing that earmarks often bypass competitive review and are awarded because of political influence rather than merit.

### Odors, stadiums and water taxis

Among the projects highlighted in the 2009 report was funding for **swine odor and manure management research**, an item critics frequently cite as an example of narrow agricultural spending. Supporters of such research say the work addresses real problems for farmers and rural communities, including air quality, waste management and public health concerns near large livestock operations.

The report also pointed to federal money connected to **Old Tiger Stadium** in Detroit, where preservation and redevelopment efforts had become a local flashpoint after the Detroit Tigers moved to Comerica Park. Critics questioned why federal taxpayers should help pay for a local stadium-related project, while supporters argued the site had historic value and redevelopment potential for the surrounding neighborhood.

Another earmark singled out by the group was funding for a **Pleasure Beach water taxi** project in Connecticut. Pleasure Beach, a barrier beach area near Bridgeport and Stratford, has limited access, and local officials have argued that transportation funding would help restore public access and support tourism. Watchdog groups, however, said the project was the type of localized benefit that should be funded at the state or municipal level, not through congressional earmarks.

### Alaska, Hawaii and the pork rankings

As in previous years, Citizens Against Government Waste ranked states by the amount of earmarked spending they received. Smaller states with powerful appropriators often ranked high when earmarks were measured on a per-capita basis.

The group’s 2009 rankings placed states such as **Alaska and Hawaii** near the top, continuing a pattern that watchdogs attribute to senior lawmakers’ influence over the appropriations process.

CAGW also singled out some of Congress’ most powerful appropriators, including lawmakers such as **Sen. Daniel Inouye of Hawaii**, **Sen. Thad Cochran of Mississippi** and **Rep. John Murtha of Pennsylvania**, who have long been associated with bringing large sums of federal money back to their states and districts.

Supporters of those lawmakers say earmarks can fund important infrastructure, defense, research and economic development projects that federal agencies might otherwise overlook. Critics counter that the system rewards seniority and political clout, not national priorities.

### Critics: earmarks undermine trust

Citizens Against Government Waste and other fiscal conservatives argue that earmarks contribute to public cynicism about Congress, particularly when projects are inserted into massive spending bills with little debate.

The group said earmarks are especially troubling during a period of rising deficits and economic uncertainty. The 2009 report was released as the federal government was spending heavily in response to the financial crisis and recession, intensifying scrutiny of all discretionary spending.

Watchdog groups also argue that earmarks can be a gateway to corruption, citing past scandals in which lobbyists or campaign contributors sought favorable treatment from lawmakers. While earmarks represent a small portion of overall federal spending, critics say they symbolize a larger problem: Congress using taxpayer money to reward local interests and political allies.

### Recipients defend the money

Recipients of earmarked funds often reject the “pork” label, saying the projects serve legitimate public purposes.

Agricultural researchers say studies on livestock odor and manure management help farmers comply with environmental rules and reduce conflicts between farms and nearby residents. Local officials involved with transportation or redevelopment projects say federal assistance can help communities complete projects they could not afford on their own.

In Connecticut, supporters of improved access to Pleasure Beach have argued that transportation funding could reconnect residents with a public recreation area. In Detroit, backers of preserving or redeveloping the Old Tiger Stadium site have described it as an effort to protect local history and spur neighborhood investment.

Those defenses reflect the broader debate over earmarks: one lawmaker’s “pork” is often another community’s infrastructure project, research grant or economic lifeline.

### Calls for reform

Congress has taken steps in recent years to require more disclosure of earmark requests, including identifying sponsors and posting requests publicly. But watchdog groups say the reforms have not gone far enough.

Citizens Against Government Waste called for eliminating earmarks entirely, arguing that federal money should be awarded through competitive, merit-based processes rather than directed by individual lawmakers.

Many members of Congress, however, have defended the practice, saying elected representatives — not federal bureaucrats — are best positioned to understand the needs of their districts and states.

The 2009 “Pig Book” underscores that the fight over earmarks remains as much about political philosophy as dollars: whether local spending decisions should be shaped by Congress’ power of the purse, or left to agencies, states and local governments.

For taxpayers, the watchdog group said, the message is simpler: even in a recession, the pork barrel is still open.

## Watchdog Group Targets Congressional “Pork” in Fiscal 2009 Spending

**WASHINGTON** — A government watchdog group is taking aim at Congress over what it calls billions of dollars in wasteful pork-barrel spending, saying lawmakers continued to steer federal money to home-state projects despite rising deficits and growing public concern over government spending.

Citizens Against Government Waste, a Washington-based taxpayer advocacy organization, released its annual **“Congressional Pig Book”** report, identifying thousands of earmarks in the fiscal year 2009 appropriations bills. The group said the report highlights how members of Congress used earmarks — funding provisions directed to specific projects, often with limited debate — to send federal dollars back to their districts and states.

According to Citizens Against Government Waste, Congress approved **10,160 earmarks costing $19.6 billion** in fiscal year 2009. The group said the total represented a continued pattern of lawmakers inserting pet projects into spending bills, even as the country faced a severe economic downturn and the federal government was committing large sums to stimulus efforts and financial-sector rescue programs.

Tom Schatz, president of Citizens Against Government Waste, said the findings showed that Congress had not changed its habits.

“At a time when taxpayers are being asked to shoulder unprecedented federal spending, Congress should be cutting waste — not adding more pork,” Schatz said in criticizing the earmark process.

The “Pig Book” has long been used by the group to name and shame lawmakers who request or benefit from earmarks. Citizens Against Government Waste defines pork-barrel projects using criteria such as whether the spending was requested by only one chamber of Congress, was not competitively awarded, was not requested by the president, or served a local or special interest rather than a national priority.

## Notable Projects Cited

Among the projects highlighted in the fiscal 2009 report were earmarks the group portrayed as questionable or unnecessary, including funding for agricultural research, local museums, and regional development programs.

The report cited examples such as:

- Funding for **swine odor and manure management research**;
- Money for specialty crop and agricultural research projects;
- Earmarks for local cultural institutions and museums;
- Funds directed to regional education, economic development, and infrastructure projects;
- Defense-related earmarks that Citizens Against Government Waste said were not requested by the Pentagon.

The watchdog group has frequently argued that while some individual projects may have local merit, the earmark process allows lawmakers to bypass normal competitive funding rules and direct taxpayer dollars based on political influence.

Schatz said that was the central problem.

“Earmarks are not about national priorities,” he said. “They are about political priorities.”

## Lawmakers Receiving the Most Earmarks

The report also singled out lawmakers associated with the largest number or dollar value of earmarks. Senior appropriators — members of the House and Senate committees that write spending bills — were again among those receiving the most attention.

According to Citizens Against Government Waste, some of the biggest earmark beneficiaries in fiscal 2009 included powerful members of Congress from both parties, including senators and representatives with senior positions on appropriations panels.

The group’s rankings placed lawmakers such as **Sen. Thad Cochran of Mississippi**, **Sen. Daniel Inouye of Hawaii**, and **Rep. John Murtha of Pennsylvania** among those associated with especially large earmark totals. All three were influential appropriators with a long history of directing federal funds to their states or districts.

Cochran, the senior Republican on the Senate Appropriations Committee at the time, was listed by the group as one of the top recipients of earmarked funds. Inouye, then the Democratic chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, was also cited for a large number of projects benefiting Hawaii. Murtha, a powerful House appropriator known for directing defense-related spending to his Pennsylvania district, was another frequent target of taxpayer watchdog groups.

Supporters of earmarks have argued that members of Congress are better positioned than federal agencies to understand local needs and that earmarks can fund valuable projects that might otherwise be overlooked. Critics counter that the process rewards political clout and encourages unnecessary spending.

## Broader Debate Over Earmarks

The fiscal 2009 “Pig Book” arrived during a period of heightened scrutiny of federal spending. The United States was in the midst of the Great Recession, and Congress had recently passed major spending measures aimed at stabilizing the economy. Against that backdrop, taxpayer groups argued that earmarks sent the wrong message.

Citizens Against Government Waste said the earmark process lacked transparency and accountability, even after reforms requiring lawmakers to disclose some earmark requests.

Schatz said disclosure alone was not enough.

“Taxpayers deserve to know who is asking for the money, where it is going, and why it is being spent,” he said. “But the ultimate goal should be to eliminate wasteful earmarks altogether.”

The report’s release renewed calls from fiscal conservatives and watchdog organizations for Congress to impose stricter limits on earmarks or ban them entirely. In later years, congressional leaders would adopt a formal earmark moratorium, though earmarks eventually returned under new transparency rules.

For Citizens Against Government Waste, the fiscal 2009 report was another warning that the earmark culture remained deeply embedded on Capitol Hill.

“Pork-barrel spending may be a small part of the overall federal budget,” Schatz said, “but it is a symbol of how Washington spends money — and why taxpayers are frustrated.”

**Watchdog Group Unveils Annual “Pig Book,” Targeting 10,160 Congressional Earmarks**

**WASHINGTON** — A government-spending watchdog group is out with its annual list of what it calls the most wasteful projects in the federal budget, spotlighting **10,160 earmarked projects** and reigniting a familiar fight on Capitol Hill over whether those local spending items are “pork” or legitimate investments.

Citizens Against Government Waste, a fiscally conservative watchdog organization, released its latest **Congressional Pig Book**, accusing lawmakers of steering billions of taxpayer dollars to pet projects with little scrutiny. The group says the earmarks identified in the report total nearly **$20 billion** in federal spending.

“This is business as usual in Washington,” CAGW President **Tom Schatz** said in releasing the report, arguing that earmarks are often inserted into spending bills without hearings, competitive bidding or meaningful debate.

Among the projects singled out by the group are some with eye-catching titles, including federal money for **swine odor and manure management research** and a grant connected to a **dinosaur museum**. CAGW says such examples illustrate how narrowly targeted spending can make its way into massive appropriations bills while taxpayers are left with the bill.

The report names both Republicans and Democrats, underscoring that earmarking has long been a bipartisan practice. Lawmakers frequently cited in Pig Book reports over the years include senior appropriators such as **Sen. Thad Cochran of Mississippi**, **Sen. Tom Harkin of Iowa**, **Rep. John Murtha of Pennsylvania**, **Rep. Charles Rangel of New York**, and Utah senators **Orrin Hatch** and **Bob Bennett**, among others, depending on the project and spending bill.

CAGW criticized money directed toward agricultural research, local museums, cultural institutions, transportation projects and economic-development grants, arguing that many would not survive a competitive merit-based review.

But supporters of the projects pushed back, saying the watchdog group often mocks projects without explaining their purpose.

Backers of the **swine odor research**, for example, argue that the work addresses real environmental and public-health concerns in agricultural communities, where large livestock operations can affect air quality, water quality and quality of life. They say research into manure management can help farmers comply with environmental rules and reduce conflicts between farms and nearby residents.

Supporters of museum and tourism-related grants also say those projects can serve a broader economic purpose. A dinosaur museum, they argue, is not merely a local attraction but part of a regional tourism strategy that can support jobs, education and scientific preservation.

Lawmakers who defend earmarks say Congress has a constitutional role in deciding how federal money is spent — and that elected representatives often know local needs better than federal agencies in Washington.

Critics counter that earmarks reward political clout, favor senior members of powerful committees and encourage backroom deal-making.

The release of the Pig Book comes as Congress continues to face pressure over deficits, debt and transparency in federal spending. While earmarks make up only a fraction of the overall federal budget, groups like CAGW argue they are a symbol of a larger problem: a spending culture in which small projects multiply into billions of dollars.

For taxpayers, the debate remains the same as ever: one district’s vital investment is another watchdog’s pork-barrel spending.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed CNN.com political article about pork-barrel spending in Congress based on the 2009 Pig Book report, including dollar amounts, specific earmarked projects, rankings by state and lawmaker, quotes from Citizens Against Government Waste, and a defense of the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy funding.

**Original CNN.com-style political article**

# Watchdog group: Congress served up $19.6 billion in “pork” in 2009 spending bills

**WASHINGTON** — Congress tucked more than 10,000 earmarks worth nearly $20 billion into the 2009 appropriations bills, according to the latest “Congressional Pig Book” released by Citizens Against Government Waste, a conservative-leaning taxpayer watchdog group that has long tracked what it calls pork-barrel spending.

The 2009 report identified **10,160 earmarks costing $19.6 billion**, a sharp reminder that even after years of bipartisan promises to rein in earmarking, lawmakers continued to direct federal dollars to favored local projects, research programs, museums, universities and economic-development efforts.

“Despite claims that Congress has cleaned up its act, the 2009 Pig Book shows that lawmakers are still spending billions of dollars on parochial projects,” Citizens Against Government Waste President **Thomas A. Schatz** said in the report’s rollout materials. CAGW argued that earmarks remain a symbol of Washington’s “pay-to-play” culture, rewarding political clout rather than national priorities.

The group’s annual “Pig Book” is one of Washington’s best-known inventories of earmarks. CAGW defines pork-barrel projects as spending items that meet at least one of several criteria, including being requested by only one chamber of Congress, not specifically authorized, not competitively awarded, not requested by the president, or serving a narrow local or special interest.

## A $19.6 billion target

CAGW said the 2009 earmark total represented an increase from the prior year, even though Congress had adopted new disclosure rules intended to make earmarks more transparent. The watchdog group said lawmakers had become better at publicly listing sponsors but had not stopped steering money home.

Among the projects highlighted in the report were:

- **$3.8 million for the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy in Detroit**
- **$1.8 million for swine odor and manure management research in Iowa**
- **$1.7 million for honey bee research**
- **$1.9 million for the Charles B. Rangel Center for Public Service in New York**
- **$2.1 million for the Center for Grape Genetics in New York**
- **$951,500 for “Sustainable Las Vegas”**
- **$380,000 for Jazz at Lincoln Center**
- **millions more for museums, agricultural research initiatives, local transportation improvements and university programs**

To CAGW, such projects illustrated the core problem: federal spending being parceled out for local priorities outside the normal competitive or agency-review process.

“Every dollar spent on pork is a dollar that is not being used to reduce the deficit, provide broad-based tax relief or fund programs that have been evaluated on the merits,” Schatz said, according to CAGW’s summary of the report.

## States with the biggest earmark hauls

The Pig Book ranked states both by total earmark dollars and by pork per capita, a metric that often boosts small states with powerful appropriators.

Large states predictably appeared near the top in total dollars, while smaller states with senior members on spending committees often ranked high per resident.

According to CAGW’s 2009 analysis, states with particularly large earmark totals included:

1. **Hawaii** — boosted by the clout of senior appropriator Sen. Daniel Inouye  
2. **Alaska** — long a major recipient of earmarked federal spending  
3. **Mississippi** — home to then-Sen. Thad Cochran, one of the Senate’s most powerful appropriators  
4. **California** — reflecting its size and large congressional delegation  
5. **New York** — with earmarks for universities, cultural institutions and local projects  

On a per-capita basis, the report pointed to states such as **Hawaii, Alaska, Mississippi, North Dakota and West Virginia** as major beneficiaries, arguing that seniority and committee assignments frequently mattered more than population or need.

CAGW has long said the pattern shows why earmarks are politically resilient: the benefits are concentrated in a district or state, while the costs are spread across taxpayers nationwide.

## Senior lawmakers drew scrutiny

The report also singled out powerful lawmakers who sponsored or helped secure large amounts of earmarked spending.

Among the members whose earmarks drew attention were:

- **Sen. Daniel Inouye, D-Hawaii**, then chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, whose state received hundreds of millions of dollars in earmarks.
- **Sen. Thad Cochran, R-Mississippi**, a senior Republican appropriator, who was associated with major earmark funding for Mississippi.
- **Rep. Charles Rangel, D-New York**, whose name was attached to the **$1.9 million Charles B. Rangel Center for Public Service** at City College of New York.
- **Michigan lawmakers**, including members who supported the **Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy** project.
- **Nevada lawmakers**, linked to earmarks such as **Sustainable Las Vegas**.

CAGW said appropriators remained the central players. Members on the House and Senate Appropriations Committees, the group argued, had an outsized ability to direct spending to home-state projects.

“Earmarks are the currency of Washington power,” CAGW said in its report, contending that members use them to reward supporters, strengthen political alliances and bring home visible projects that can be touted to voters.

## Old Tiger Stadium funding draws criticism — and a defense

One of the more visible earmarks in the 2009 Pig Book was **$3.8 million for the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy**, a Detroit nonprofit effort aimed at preserving portions of the historic ballpark site and converting it into a community asset.

To CAGW, the project was an example of a local preservation effort that should be funded by local government, private donors or philanthropic organizations — not federal taxpayers. The group questioned why residents outside Michigan should contribute to the redevelopment of a former baseball stadium.

But supporters of the Old Tiger Stadium Conservancy have defended the funding as more than nostalgia. They argue the site was an important piece of Detroit’s history and that federal assistance could help transform a decaying landmark into public space, youth athletic fields and a neighborhood redevelopment anchor.

Backers have said the project would preserve the historic playing field and portions of the stadium’s legacy while creating a usable community resource in Corktown, one of Detroit’s oldest neighborhoods. They also argued that the federal dollars could leverage private donations and local investment at a time when Detroit was facing severe economic stress.

In that view, the earmark was not simply a subsidy for baseball history but an economic-development and historic-preservation project in a city struggling with population loss, budget pressure and abandoned property.

The dispute captured the broader earmark debate: one lawmaker’s pork is often another community’s preservation plan, job creator or civic investment.

## Earmarks under fire from both parties

By 2009, earmarks had become a bipartisan political liability. Republicans frequently attacked Democrats for excess spending, while Democrats pointed out that GOP lawmakers had long used earmarks aggressively when they controlled Congress.

Both parties contained members who pledged to give up earmarks — and both parties contained appropriators who defended the practice as a constitutional power of Congress.

Supporters of earmarks argue that elected representatives know their districts better than federal agencies do. They say Congress has the authority to direct spending and that local projects should not be left entirely to unelected bureaucrats.

Critics counter that earmarks encourage waste, secrecy and favoritism. They say even relatively small earmarks can help grease the wheels for massive spending bills by giving individual lawmakers a reason to vote yes.

CAGW said the 2009 Pig Book proved that disclosure alone was not enough.

“Transparency is important, but transparency does not make wasteful spending acceptable,” Schatz said. “Taxpayers deserve fewer earmarks, not merely better-labeled earmarks.”

## The politics of pork

The Pig Book’s release came as Washington was already debating deficits, the financial crisis, bank bailouts and the size of the federal government. Against that backdrop, CAGW sought to frame earmarks as a test of whether Congress was serious about fiscal discipline.

The total — **$19.6 billion** — represented a small fraction of overall federal spending, but watchdog groups said earmarks have symbolic importance because they reveal how Congress sets priorities.

CAGW also argued that earmarks can distort agency budgets. For example, when Congress directs money to a specific university research center, museum or local infrastructure project, agencies may have less flexibility to fund projects through competitive grant processes.

The report’s agricultural earmarks were a frequent target. Projects such as **swine odor and manure management research**, **honey bee research** and **grape genetics research** may have scientific or economic value, but CAGW questioned why they were singled out through congressional direction rather than competing for funding.

Cultural earmarks drew similar scrutiny. Funding for institutions such as **Jazz at Lincoln Center** or stadium preservation projects may be popular locally, but the watchdog group said such spending raises questions about national responsibility and fiscal priorities.

## A familiar Washington fight

The 2009 Pig Book did not end the earmark debate, but it added pressure to a growing reform movement. Within a few years, Congress would adopt an earmark moratorium, though lawmakers later revived congressionally directed spending under new rules and public disclosure requirements.

CAGW has continued to argue that earmarks are inherently prone to abuse, regardless of transparency reforms. Supporters continue to insist that properly disclosed earmarks are a legitimate way for Congress to respond to local needs.

The 2009 report showed why the issue remains so politically durable. Earmarks are easy to attack in the abstract but often popular when attached to a recognizable local project — a university lab, a transportation fix, a museum, a redevelopment site or a historic ballpark.

For taxpayers, CAGW said, the bottom line was simple: **10,160 earmarks, $19.6 billion, and a Congress still unwilling to give up pork.**
